title: The Three Conjugations
summary: The present tense completed: the second and third conjugations beside the first, how the stem is got from the principal parts, the verbs of wanting and being able with their infinitives, and the adverbs of frequency that go with the present.

rules.heading: Getting the Present Stem
rules.statement: Every present form is built on the **present stem**, which is got by removing the ending of the third person present — the second of the three principal parts (¶23). *dirba* gives the stem *dirb-*, *turi* gives *tur-*, *skaito* gives *skait-*. Because the third person is cited in every dictionary, no present form ever has to be guessed.

rules.heading: The Second Conjugation
rules.statement: Verbs whose third person present ends in **-i** take the endings below. The first person singular is **-iu**, not *-u*; and the second person singular is identical to the third, so that *tu turi* and *jis turi* differ only in their pronoun — one of the few places where the pronoun cannot be dropped without loss.

rules.heading: The Third Conjugation
rules.statement: Verbs whose third person present ends in **-o** take the endings below. Here the first and second persons singular are **-au** and **-ai**, and they are never confused with anything else; the third person in -o is the mark of the whole class.

rules.heading: The Three Conjugations Compared
rules.statement: Set side by side, the three differ only in the vowel that runs through them — **a**, **i**, **o**. The plural endings are built alike in all three: the third-person form plus *-me* and *-te*. Learn the third person and the rest follows.

paradigms.caption: The present tense in full
paradigms.footnote: In every conjugation one form serves the whole third person, and the plural is the third person plus -me or -te.

examples.gloss: I live in Vilnius and work.

rules.heading: Wanting and Liking, and the Cases They Govern
rules.statement: Two very common verbs differ in the case they take, and the difference must be learned with them. **Norėti**, to want, governs the **genitive**; **mėgti**, to like, governs the **accusative**. The reason is the old one: what is wanted is not yet had, and so is a part rather than a whole, while what is liked is liked entire.

examples.target: Ji nori duonos, bet mėgsta obuolius.
examples.gloss: She wants bread, but likes apples.

footnotes: *klausyti*, to listen to, likewise governs the genitive: *klausau muzikos*, I am listening to music.

rules.heading: The Complementary Infinitive
rules.statement: **Galėti** (to be able), **norėti** (to want) and **mėgti** (to like) may be completed by an **infinitive** instead of by a noun. The infinitive ends in *-ti* and never changes; the finite verb alone carries the person. Note that when *norėti* is completed by an infinitive there is no noun to put in the genitive, and the question of case does not arise.

rules.heading: Adverbs of Frequency
rules.statement: Because Lithuanian has one present tense where English has two (¶24), how often an action happens is said with an **adverb** rather than with a change of tense: *visada* (always), *dažnai* (often), *kartais* (sometimes), *retai* (rarely), *niekada* (never). They stand before the verb. **Niekada** requires the verb to be negated as well — Lithuanian doubles its negatives where English refuses to.
footnotes: The double negative is obligatory, not emphatic: *niekada valgome* is simply ungrammatical.

vocabulary.notes: Requires the verb to be negated as well.

drills.explanation: The second conjugation takes -iu in the first person singular, not the -u of the first conjugation. *turi* serves both *tu* and the whole third person.
The third conjugation takes -ai in the second person singular. *skaitau* is the first person and *skaito* the third.
*norėti* is of the second conjugation, so the first person is *noriu*. The genitive *kavos* is what *norėti* governs (¶39).

drills.stem: A dictionary gives **klausyti, klauso, klausė**. Which conjugation is it, and what is the present stem?
drills.explanation: The third person present *klauso* ends in -o, which names the third conjugation, and removing that ending leaves the stem *klaus-*. The infinitive tells you nothing about the conjugation.
*norėti* governs the genitive and *mėgti* the accusative, so the second and fourth have their cases exchanged: *mėgstu kavą*, *nori obuolių*.
Only the finite verb carries the person; what completes it stays in the infinitive. Two finite verbs in a row is impossible, and *darbą* is a noun where a verb is wanted.

drills.stem: *Ji ____ studijuoja.* Which adverbs could fill the gap as the sentence stands?
drills.explanation: *niekada* cannot: it requires the verb to be negated as well, giving *Ji niekada nestudijuoja*. Lithuanian doubles its negatives where English will not.

drills.stem: *Tu turi* and *jis turi* are identical. Why can the pronoun not be dropped here, when it usually can?
options: Because in the second conjugation the second and third persons singular fall together, so only the pronoun tells them apart.
Because the second conjugation has no personal endings.
drills.explanation: Normally the ending names the person and the pronoun is left out (¶24). In the second conjugation *-i* serves *tu*, *jis*, *ji*, *jie* and *jos* alike, so the ending has nothing left to say and the pronoun must carry the sense.

drills.stem: Of the verbs *dirbti, turėti, skaityti, mėgti*, which take **-ame** or **-ome** in the first person plural?
drills.explanation: The plural is the third-person form plus -me: *dirba* → *dirbame*, *skaito* → *skaitome*, *mėgsta* → *mėgstame*. Only *turėti*, of the second conjugation, gives *turime*. Note that *mėgti* belongs to the first conjugation despite its infinitive, its third person being *mėgsta*.

drills.stem: **Ji nori obuolio.** How many words change form if *ji* is replaced by *jie* and the verb by *mėgti*?
drills.explanation: Two: *nori* → *mėgsta*, and *obuolio* → *obuolį*, because *mėgti* governs the accusative where *norėti* governed the genitive (¶39). The third person is one form for both numbers, so changing *ji* to *jie* changes the verb not at all.

drills.title: Rūtos diena
drills.passage: Rūta gyvena Vilniuje. Ji studijuoja universitete ir dirba kavinėje. Rūta mėgsta muziką ir dažnai klauso muzikos. Vakare ji nori skaityti, bet kartais žiūri televizorių. Ji niekada nevalgo duonos be sviesto. Rūta gerai kalba lietuviškai ir supranta angliškai.
drills.translation: Rūta lives in Vilnius. She studies at the university and works in a café. Rūta likes music and often listens to music. In the evening she wants to read, but sometimes she watches television. She never eats bread without butter. Rūta speaks Lithuanian well and understands English.

questions.explanation: *Rūta mėgsta muziką* — *mėgti* governs the accusative. *muzikos* is the genitive the passage uses after *klauso*, which governs the genitive instead.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs in the passage belong to the **second** conjugation?
questions.explanation: *nori* and *žiūri* end in -i and so belong to the second conjugation. *gyvena* in -a is the first and *klauso* in -o the third.

questions.stem: The passage says **Ji niekada nevalgo duonos.** How many words would change form if *niekada* were replaced by *dažnai*?
questions.explanation: Two: *nevalgo* → *valgo*, since only *niekada* required the negative, and *duonos* → *duoną*, the object leaving the genitive of negation for the accusative (¶31). Answering one forgets that the case of the object hangs on the negation.
